title: Black Cells in Four Rows
statement: Each cell of a grid with $4$ rows and $9$ columns is coloured black or white. The rows are numbered $1, 2, 3, 4$ from top to bottom, and two colourings are counted as different if some cell has a different colour in each, so rotations and reflections are not identified. Say that two rows meet in a column if both of their cells in that column are black. A colouring is valid if each of the row pairs $(1,2)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,4)$ and $(4,1)$ meets in exactly one column. No condition is placed on the row pairs $(1,3)$ and $(2,4)$. There are $T$ valid colourings. What remainder does $T$ leave on division by $1000$?
hints: Look at a single column. For each of the $16$ possible sets of black cells, list which of the four required row pairs $(1,2)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,4)$, $(4,1)$ meet in that column. Some columns give no meeting, and some give several.

Draw rows $1, 2, 3, 4$ as the vertices of a $4$-cycle, whose edges are the four required pairs. A column's black set covers each edge with both endpoints black. Each edge must be covered by exactly one column, so use casework on how the four edges are split into blocks, where each block is the set of edges covered by one column.

On the $4$-cycle whose edges are the required pairs, seven column patterns cover no edge. A block can be one edge (two adjacent black rows), two adjacent edges (three black rows) or all four edges (four black rows), and each block comes from exactly one pattern. The edge partitions are: $1$ with four single edges, $4$ with one adjacent pair and two single edges, $2$ with two adjacent pairs, and $1$ with the whole cycle. A partition with $k$ blocks gives $9 \cdot 8 \cdots (9-k+1) \cdot 7^{9-k}$ colourings. It remains to add these contributions and reduce modulo $1000$.
solution: View rows $1, 2, 3, 4$ as the vertices of a $4$-cycle with edges $a = (1,2)$, $b = (2,3)$, $c = (3,4)$, $d = (4,1)$. A column covers an edge if both of that edge's rows are black in the column. A colouring is valid exactly when each edge is covered by exactly one column. Sort the $16$ possible columns by the edges they cover. No edge: all white, one black cell ($4$ ways), rows $\{1,3\}$ or rows $\{2,4\}$. This gives $7$ free patterns. One edge: two adjacent black rows, with one pattern for each edge. Two adjacent edges: three black rows, with one pattern for each of $\{a,b\}$, $\{b,c\}$, $\{c,d\}$, $\{d,a\}$. All four edges: all four rows black, which is one pattern. These account for $7 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 16$ patterns. So the possible non-empty covered sets, which we call blocks, are single edges, adjacent pairs of edges and the whole cycle, and each block comes from exactly one pattern. In a valid colouring, the blocks of the non-free columns are disjoint and together contain all four edges, so they form a partition of $\{a,b,c,d\}$ into blocks. Conversely, take such a partition with $k$ blocks. Placing its blocks' patterns in $k$ distinct columns and free patterns in all other columns gives a valid colouring. The blocks are different sets, so there are $9 \cdot 8 \cdots (9-k+1)$ placements, and the other columns can be filled in $7^{9-k}$ ways. Each valid colouring arises from exactly one partition and one placement. Now count the partitions. If the whole cycle is a block, there is $1$ partition, with $k = 1$. Otherwise all blocks have size $1$ or $2$. With no adjacent pair there is $1$ partition, with $k = 4$. With exactly one adjacent pair there are $4$ partitions, with $k = 3$. With two adjacent pairs, they must be disjoint, so they are $\{a,b\},\{c,d\}$ or $\{b,c\},\{d,a\}$. This gives $2$ partitions, with $k = 2$. Therefore $$T = 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 7^5 + 4 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 7^6 + 2 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7^7 + 9 \cdot 7^8.$$ The four terms are $50\,824\,368$, $237\,180\,384$, $118\,590\,192$ and $51\,883\,209$, so $T = 458\,478\,153$. The remainder when $T$ is divided by $1000$ is $153$. Why this works. casework, graph-modeling, rule-of-product: a single column can supply several meetings, so modelling the required pairs as a $4$-cycle reduces the count to cases on edge partitions, each of which is a simple product of column choices.
